text: This closing lesson is about the skill that matters most from this entire course: writing up what you actually found, accurately, in a way that neither oversells nor undersells a real result.

A trustworthy write-up needs five things, stated explicitly. The exact setup: dataset, feature count, qubit count, encoding choice, ansatz, and how many iterations and samples were actually used. The exact classical baseline, and how it was chosen. The exact measured numbers, not rounded up or cherry-picked. What varied between runs that could explain the result. And an explicit statement of what does and doesn't generalize.

Applying that template here: the setup was real Iris data, two features, two qubits, angle encoding, a one-layer ansatz, and honestly, only one gradient step on one training sample. The baseline was a genuinely simple, un-weakened 2.5 centimeter threshold rule. The measured numbers: the classical baseline scored 100 percent, six out of six, while the quantum classifier scored 50 percent, three out of six.

What this result accurately says is narrow: a quantum classifier trained on one sample for one step underperformed a trivial classical rule on this specific task — close to self-evident, not surprising. What it does not say is that quantum classifiers underperform classical ones on Iris-like tasks in general, since a properly multi-sample-trained version would very plausibly close most of the gap. This closes the loop back to Lesson 1's calibrated uncertainty, applied honestly to your own result.

This course opened by calling quantum machine learning an open research question and asked you to hold calibrated uncertainty rather than hype or dismissal. You built something real, measured it against a fair baseline, got a result that didn't flatter the quantum approach, and reported exactly why — the actual, transferable skill this course was built to teach.
